entities.name: Temple of Ephesian Artemis
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus (Greek: Ἀρτεμίσιον, Artemision), situated in ancient Ephesus (modern Selçuk, Turkey), was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World — a colossal Ionic temple dedicated to the goddess Artemis that reached its most magnificent form circa 550 BCE under Lydian King Croesus's patronage, measuring approximately 115 meters long by 55 meters wide with 127 columns standing 18 meters high, and making it the largest building in the Greek world for several centuries until surpassed by the Parthenon.

The Artemision had several iterations. An earlier archaic temple was destroyed by a catastrophic flood circa 600 BCE; the famous version funded by King Croesus (whose wealth was proverbial) was constructed from around 560 BCE and took approximately 120 years to complete, with contributions from artists including the sculptor Scopas. The temple was destroyed by arson on July 21, 356 BCE — the same night, according to the Roman historian Plutarch, that Alexander the Great was born — by Herostratus, who wished to achieve immortality through infamy. Alexander himself later offered to pay for its reconstruction on his campaigns through the region.

A third version was rebuilt after Herostratus's destruction, standing until its plunder by the Gothic peoples in 262 CE and final demolition when Christianity became the Roman Empire's religion in the late 4th century CE. Today only a single reconstructed column marks the site. The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus represents the apex of archaic Greek religious architecture and the ambition of ancient sacred building programs.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus — one of the Seven Wonders, the largest Greek building of its era, destroyed by arson for fame and eventually by Christian religious transformation — is both a supreme achievement of ancient sacred architecture and a paradigmatic tale of human ambition and destruction.
